The true story of Richard Williams, who raised his daughters Venus and Serena in Compton, California, with an unconventional training plan and unshakeable belief that they would become the greatest tennis players in the world. Will Smith's warm, generous performance drives this crowd-pleasing celebration of an extraordinary family.

In 1960s Belfast, a young boy navigates his Protestant community's eruption into violence at the beginning of the Troubles, while his beloved grandfather declines and his family considers emigrating. Kenneth Branagh's autobiographical film is a love letter to a lost childhood, shot in luminous black and white.

A pair of scientists discover that a massive comet is on a collision course with Earth, and embark on a media tour to warn humanity — only to find that no one wants to hear bad news. Adam McKay's savage, frequently funny satire uses the end of the world as a metaphor for climate change and the media's inability to process existential threats.

In 1940s America, a carnival psychiatrist and a small-time mentalist con artist become entangled with a beautiful, dangerous society woman while running an elaborate psychic fraud on the wealthy. Guillermo del Toro's gorgeous, morally serious noir remake is a beautifully crafted study of manipulation, hubris, and self-destruction.

On a New Zealand ranch in the 1920s, a charismatic, intimidating rancher bullies his gentle brother and is disturbed by the arrival of the brother's new wife and her sensitive young son. Jane Campion's slow-burn psychological Western is a masterful, deeply unsettling exploration of repressed desire and its violence.

The star-crossed love between Tony, a former Jet, and Maria, sister of the Sharks' leader, unfolds against the backdrop of fierce gang rivalry between Puerto Rican and white teenagers in 1950s New York City. Spielberg's technically ravishing revival of the Bernstein-Sondheim musical is also a significant improvement on the 1961 original.

A first-generation Chinese-American woman and her immigrant mother discover they can access the memories and skills of their parallel universe selves, and must save the multiverse from a nihilistic villain who turns out to be their own daughter. The Daniels' wildly inventive, maximalist film uses its absurdist premise to deliver a genuinely moving story about acceptance and love.

Retired naval aviator Pete 'Maverick' Mitchell is called back to train a new generation of Top Gun pilots for a seemingly impossible mission, confronting his past and the limits of his recklessness. Joseph Kosinski's sequel is a masterclass in crowd-pleasing blockbuster filmmaking, with practical aerial sequences of breathtaking technical ambition.

A semi-autobiographical portrait of Steven Spielberg's childhood in 1950s Arizona, as the young Sammy Fabelman discovers filmmaking, watches his family fracture, and learns a devastating secret about his parents' marriage. Spielberg's most personal film is a tender, funny, and deeply moving meditation on art, family, and the complicated love of parents.

On a remote Irish island, a musician abruptly ends his lifelong friendship with a man he simply doesn't enjoy talking to anymore, and the devastated friend refuses to accept the rejection. Martin McDonagh's melancholy, darkly funny fable uses the end of a friendship to meditate on creative ambition, connection, and the pointless violence of male pride.

movie_title: All Quiet on the Western Front
synopsis: In the final months of World War I, a young German soldier experiences the horrors of the Western Front, losing friends and his own innocence in a war he is beginning to understand was never worth fighting. Edward Berger's stunning, unsparing remake of the 1930 classic is a devastating antiwar statement filmed with brutal physical immediacy.

A world-renowned female conductor at the peak of her career begins to unravel as accusations from a former pupil emerge, forcing a reckoning with her use of power and the contradictions between her art and her life. Todd Field's commanding, formally assured film is anchored by Cate Blanchett's extraordinary, multivalent performance.

The life of Elvis Presley is told through the eyes of his enigmatic manager, Colonel Tom Parker, tracing the singer's journey from poor Southern boy to cultural icon and eventual captive of his own fame. Baz Luhrmann's kinetic, overwhelming biopic features Austin Butler's remarkable star-making performance as Elvis.

A satire of class and entitlement set aboard a luxury cruise ship, where a violent storm traps a group of the ultra-wealthy with a seasick Marxist captain, until they wash up on a desert island where the social order completely inverts. Ruben Östlund's wickedly funny, pointed film is the most playful examination of class warfare since Parasite.

In a remote Mennonite community, after a series of violent sexual assaults are revealed to have been committed by men in the colony, the women gather secretly to decide: do nothing, stay and fight, or leave. Sarah Polley's formally austere, quietly devastating film is a profound meditation on autonomy, faith, and collective action.

The story of J. Robert Oppenheimer, the theoretical physicist who led the Manhattan Project and built the atomic bomb, and the subsequent government hearing that destroyed his reputation. Christopher Nolan's audacious, three-hour epic is at once a thriller, a tragedy, and a meditation on scientific responsibility and political betrayal.

The story of Leonard Bernstein — composer, conductor, and musical titan — told primarily through his complicated, passionate, and often painful marriage to actress Felicia Montealegre. Bradley Cooper's formally ambitious biopic is a love story about two brilliant people navigating the distance between a man's public genius and his private life.

A Black novelist whose satirical work about inner-city life is rejected for being too literary finds his fortunes change when his agent submits a deliberately terrible 'street lit' novel under a pseudonym — and it becomes a sensation. Cord Jefferson's sharp, funny debut feature is a layered, intelligent satire about race, authenticity, and the publishing industry.

An innocent young woman created by a mad scientist in Victorian England discovers herself to be growing rapidly in intelligence and experience, and sets out to explore the world with reckless, amoral curiosity. Yorgos Lanthimos's wickedly funny, visually ravishing film is a feminist Frankenstein story and a celebration of female autonomy.

Barbie is unexpectedly struck by thoughts of death and is expelled from Barbieland, setting off a journey to the real world — with Ken in tow — that leads to an existential crisis about what it means to be human. Greta Gerwig's smartly subversive, visually delirious blockbuster uses the world's most famous doll to explore the impossible expectations placed on women.

Childhood friends Nora and Hae Sung, separated when Nora's family emigrates from South Korea to America, meet again in New York twelve years later when Nora is in a relationship with an American, and all three must navigate what might have been. Celine Song's quiet, aching debut is one of the most precise and emotionally devastating films about the roads not taken.

At a New England boarding school over Thanksgiving break, a grumpy classics teacher is assigned to supervise the few students who can't go home, including a brilliant, lonely misfit — and an unexpected, prickly friendship develops. Alexander Payne's warmly observed film is a beautifully crafted study of isolation, mentorship, and the small ways people save each other.

A celebrated German-French author is found dead at the bottom of a snowy staircase, and her husband — who survived the fall — is put on trial for murder in a case with no witnesses and mountains of ambiguity. Justine Triet's riveting, formally ingenious film uses the mechanics of a courtroom thriller to explore the unknowability of other people's lives.

In the early 20th century, the Osage Nation of Oklahoma is systematically murdered for their oil wealth in a conspiracy involving white settlers and the federal government, investigated by the newly formed FBI. Scorsese's vast, morally serious epic is told from the inside of the conspiracy, forcing us to sit with complicity and love in the same story.

A commandant of the Nazi concentration camp at Auschwitz lives with his family in a comfortable house next to the camp walls, conducting his efficient work while his wife tends her garden. Jonathan Glazer's devastating, formally radical film refuses to show the horror directly — what is heard through the walls is more terrifying than anything that could be shown.

Anora, a young Brooklyn sex worker, impulsively marries the son of a Russian oligarch, only for the wedding to be violently undone when his family's fixers arrive to annul it. Sean Baker's raucous, tender, and heartbreaking Palme d'Or winner is a screwball comedy about class, power, and the persistent, foolish hope of love.

Hungarian-Jewish architect László Tóth emigrates to America after surviving the Holocaust and slowly rebuilds his reputation designing a grand cultural center for a wealthy Pennsylvania industrialist, in a story that spans thirty years. Brady Corbet's monumental, three-and-a-half-hour film is an epic about art, survival, the American dream, and the impossible cost of creation.

The story of how Bob Dylan transformed from a folk musician named Robert Zimmerman into a generational voice in 1960s Greenwich Village, and his controversial decision to go electric at Newport in 1965. James Mangold's energetic, affectionate biopic features a career-best Timothée Chalamet in a performance of remarkable physical and vocal commitment.

When the Pope dies suddenly, the sequestered cardinals gathered to elect a new leader begin to reveal shocking secrets that call into question the very nature of the institution they serve. Edward Berger's elegant, tense drama is a sophisticated thriller about faith, power, and the human need for certainty.

In Mexico, a cartel lawyer helps a feared drug lord fake her death, transition to a new gender identity, and rebuild a criminal empire as a respectable citizen, with complex, dangerous consequences. Jacques Audiard's genre-bending, boldly artificial musical thriller is one of cinema's most formally audacious films in years.

Two Black boys at a segregated reform school in 1960s Florida endure systematic abuse, and the film moves between past and present as one survivor uncovers the truth about what happened. RaMell Ross's formally revolutionary film uses unconventional cinematography to put us inside the subjective experience of its characters in an unprecedented way.

The true story of Eunice Paiva, a Brazilian woman whose husband was disappeared by the military dictatorship in 1971, and her decades-long fight to find the truth and secure official recognition of what happened to him. Walter Salles's emotionally powerful film won Brazil the Oscar for Best International Feature Film.

A former celebrity injects herself with a substance that creates an alternate, idealized version of herself, beginning a horrifying battle for dominance between the original and her beautiful double. Coralie Fargeat's visceral, provocative body-horror film is an extreme, formally uncompromising satire about the beauty industry and society's destruction of aging women.

Based on the beloved stage musical, the young witch Elphaba and the popular Glinda forge an unlikely friendship at Shiz University before their destinies lead them toward the events of The Wizard of Oz. Jon M. Chu's spectacular first installment lavishes extraordinary production design and two powerhouse performances on Wicked's first half.

On September 5, 1972, an ABC Sports crew finds itself broadcasting the terrorist attack on Israeli athletes at the Munich Olympics live, forced to make real-time decisions about what to show and what to withhold. Tim Fehlbaum's taut, claustrophobic thriller raises urgent questions about the media's role in amplifying — and potentially enabling — acts of terror.
